newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Gilt curve to flatten on UK budget.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Gilt curve to flatten on UK budget.

text.p: Whatever British Chancellor Gordon Brown dishes up in Wednesday's budget, the chances are the gilt curve will continue to flatten, and may even invert, analysts said on Tuesday.
So investors willing to dip into the market before the budget should head for the long end of the curve for the best returns.
"Whatever happens in the budget, you can rely on the UK curve continuing to flatten and it maybe even invert," said David Boal, head of J.P. Morgan sterling securities in London.
He said a tight budget would mean a more favourable public sector borrowing profile which would entice domestic investors to hoard long gilts.
"So the curve would tend to flatten and even invert, certainly at the long end on that," said Boal.
But a looser than expected budget would leave the market looking to the Bank of England to take up the slack and raise interest rates by more than the market currently anticipates.

"That will make the curve flatten too," said Boal. "So if the budget is tight, yields will fall, if it is loose, yields will rise. Either way, there's a very strong probability the curve will invert."
At 1125 GMT, two-year notes were already yielding only 18 basis points less than 25-year gilts.
Analysts expect Brown to tighten fiscal policy by around four billion pounds when he presents his first budget on Wednesday.
But some economists say this will not be enough to take the heat out of the simmering British economy, and will leave the Bank of England to raise interest rates further.
The next monetary policy meeting is on July 9 and 10.
Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW, agreed if the Chancellor shrinks from delivering a tight budget on Wednesday, it will be up to the Bank of England to tighten the screws on the economy.
"Either way, the gilt curve will be subject to further flattening pressure, and we may even think of inversion," he said.
Adams suggested one of two strategies for gilts investors going into the budget.
"The cautious one would be to do a butterfly trade and sell your holdings of 10-year paper and buy both the long end and the short end in anticipation of curve flattening," he said.
"Or if you want to be more aggressive than that, you could just move out to the longer end of the curve."

Analysts said one risk to the flattening scenario was if the budget is just loose enough to prompt the degree of monetary tightening already factored into the short end, but is still slack enough to disappoint at the long end.
"If Brown doesn't increase taxes by as much as the market is expecting, both the short end and long end will be disappointed," said Steve Scott, gilts analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
He recommended moving down the curve as a defensive move.
Another potential upset to flattening is if the budget is so tight, the need for further monetary tightening is reduced.

"One thing to interrupt (the flattening) is if the budget is so tight, the market has to make a more optimistic interpretation of monetary policy and assume no more monetary tightening," said Boal. "Then the short end would be more positive."
Scott said the 10-year gilt/Bund spread would continue to narrow in the medium to longer term, but added in the short term, a rise in volatility may take its toll.
"So we'd recommend taking some profits but retaining some position," he said. "So if the tax increases are lower than expected, then you'd put the position back on at a higher spread level."
Scott said a move to 155 to 160 on the spread would be a good buying level for gilts against Bunds. By 1141 GMT, the spread was at 147 basis points.
"But by the year end, it could go to 115, 120," Scott added.
